title: Eleven Seconds
passages:
The barge's smudge was gone from the slate's horizon, swallowed by rain and the dark water east of the Marrow. Wren stayed at the winch. The drum sat cold, the spliced line coiled neat as a sleeping snake, and the wheelhouse speaker hissed with Salas's ghost-call on the backup channel — *keep going... tell the kid* — but the sound that wouldn't leave her was the way he'd said her name. Not *reader* or *tech* or *hey you*. *Wren*. Like he knew her. Like she'd sworn him something.

Behind her, voices rose and fell in the galley. Sol and Rusk's parting words, Dey's jaw working, Nia's flat refusal to be moved. The storm was still hours out, but the air had that charge, the pressure drop that made your teeth ache. Wren's thumb hovered over the edit wheel. She'd rebuilt hundreds of lost hours. Divers came up hollow, their slates full of static and pressure spikes, and she stitched the gaps with deck audio, suit telemetry, the rhythm of a breath held too long. She'd never once run a build on herself.

Her slate was a cracked Gen-3 reader, salt-scored and held together with tape and stubbornness. She thumbed the build key, spoke the command: *"Self. Full spool. Last descent."* The machine didn't argue. It never did. A progress bar bloomed, green and patient, pulling telemetry from a dive her body had made and her mind had never seen.

Depth trace. Heart rate. Scrubber efficiency. Time stamps marching backward from the surface — *00:00, -00:12, -00:47* — into water she didn't remember. The suit's headlamp log showed a beam cutting green at twenty meters, thirty, thirty-five. Her own voice on the comms, calm and professional: *"Reader to surface. At pocket. Seal intact."* The build kept spooling.

The build kept spooling. Then it stopped.

Not a fade, not the ragged fuzz of a suit losing pressure. A clean break. The depth trace ran down to thirty-nine meters and then simply wasn't there, and eleven seconds later it picked back up at thirty-nine meters like nothing had happened between, like the water had held still and polite. Wren had spent her whole working life learning the difference between a machine forgetting and a hand deciding. Water made dropouts soft — data smeared at the edges where a wet contact chattered, the line gone shaggy and uncertain. This was surgical. Flat walls on both sides. Somebody had reached into her body's own record, lifted eleven seconds out of it, and pressed the two ends together so clean you'd never feel the seam unless you already knew to look.

She knew to look. She'd made this exact cut two hours ago.

She could still feel where the edit wheel had sat under her thumb, that small dry resistance, when she'd taken Sol's hour — the moment at the rail, the captain choosing the two children over the twelve thousand and the Factor's drone grinding itself to scrap against the drum. She'd trimmed it out so clean Sol would surface peaceful and never know what she'd traded away. That had been mercy. That had been the job. She told herself that in the same voice she always did, the one that made it sound like stitching a wound and not like lying.

But this hole was the same shape. Same length. Eleven seconds, flat-edged, deliberate, pressed shut by a hand that knew precisely what it was doing. The machine had no opinion. It just laid the two windows on the slate for her, glowing side by side, the one she'd carved tonight and the one that had been sitting inside her own dive for who knew how long, and they matched the way two halves of the same coin match.

She pulled the timestamp on her cut. Last night. The suit had recorded a descent — *Reader to surface, at pocket, seal intact* — and somewhere in the middle of being down there in the dark at thirty-nine meters, her body had reached up and deleted eleven seconds of itself, then swum home and let her forget she'd gone. She had never once run a build on herself. She'd told people that like a boast. The reader who rebuilds everyone else's lost hours. And the reason she'd never run one was sitting right here, cut clean, waiting for her the whole time she wasn't looking.

Her thumb found the play control on the first window. The one that wasn't hers to have made. The one her body made without her, the same steady way she'd cut Sol.

She'd cut the captain to be kind. She didn't remember cutting herself at all.

Out in the dark west, patient as a metronome, Salas said her name again.

Nobody on the Marrow answered him. The man was four hundred meters of black water west and a year dead by every account that mattered, and the only one aboard who could have said why a dead man's voice knew her was hunched over her slate with eleven seconds cut clean out of her own life.

Dey's crate sat against the winch housing. The rig lay open across his knees — his salvage rebreather, the closed-circuit set that scrubbed the carbon dioxide out of the air a diver had already breathed so he could go back down on it. He'd gutted it to the frame. The scrubber canister, the cartridge of gray soda lime that ate the CO2, sat in Teo's chest instead, and without it the rig was a cage of empty hose and a mouthpiece that handed you nothing worth having past a couple meters.

He'd stopped fixing it. Wren knew the difference the way she knew a cut from a dropout. His hands had gone still on the manifold. Rusk's map was spread flat beside the wreck, the grease-pencil cross at forty-two meters, the hospital tower sketched in hard little blocks, and Dey had run the coiled spliced line out along the deck with his heel, laying it against the map, counting the gap between the Marrow and the tower. The line paid to the end of the drum and quit, stopped in the water a long way short of the mark.

"Twenty-two meters of line," Nia said. She stood in the galley door with her arms crossed, watching him count it. "Twenty-five if the drum runs clean. That's your reach. Forty-two is twice that down and twice that west, and you've got one breath in you to do it, because your air's in the kid's chest."

"One breath's more than nothing," Dey said.

"One breath is nothing, past thirty." She didn't raise her voice. She never did. "You want to know what a lungful does to a man at forty-two? It lies to him. Bottom's got your chest in a fist, all that air squeezed up tight, and it feels like plenty. Feels like you could stay the whole day. Then you turn for the top." She lifted a flat hand, slow, up toward the boom. "Every meter you rise, the air in you swells back out and goes thin, and the good part goes so thin your lights just go out. Not tired. Out. Ten meters down, in water you could stand up in, and you sink back for good. I've hauled two of them up by the collar. Both went down breathing easy."

Dey didn't look at her. He looked at the map.

In the wheelhouse door Teo was breathing too fast, the shallow quick pant of a boy counting his own breaths without meaning to, one hand curled around the last cartridge like a coin he could spend. *I'm not worth a man in the water,* he said, or tried to; it came out short and folded in the middle by his lungs. Nobody picked it up. Saying it out loud would have made it a thing they had to answer.

Wren's slate glowed on the drum housing where she'd set it. Two windows, side by side. Sol's hour and her own, cut to the same clean length. She hadn't touched it in a while. She was looking at it now the way you look at a stair that was there the whole time and you never saw.

Dey set the map down. He leaned in close, close enough to keep his voice under the wind and under Salas's patient calling, just for her.

"Wren." Low. "A body make forty-two on one breath. And come back up it."

Behind him the spliced line lay coiled and slack. The drum sat cold. Out west the dead man said her name like he'd been promised something, and Wren looked into the flat clean edge of the hole in herself, and she didn't say no.

She didn't answer Dey. Answering meant choosing, and every choice on this boat tonight cost somebody a body, and she was fresh out of bodies to spend. "Ask Nia," she said. "She's the one who's counted the men who didn't come back." Then she turned to the slate, because the other option was looking at him, and she couldn't afford that yet.

Filling a gap was the whole job. A suit lost eleven seconds to a wet contact, you didn't guess at it — you triangulated. You laid the diver's telemetry against the deck log, the ambient recording that ran off the wheelhouse mic all night, every pump and winch and argument aboard the Marrow, and you found the eleven seconds in the noise around the diver. Somebody coughed. The drum turned. A voice said a name. You built the hole back out of the world it happened in. That was the trick she'd sold a hundred hollow divers: the body keeps the record, even when you don't. The water takes the memory. It does not take the tape.

She pulled the deck log to last night. Scrubbed to the timestamp on her own cut. She'd fill her eleven seconds with whatever the Marrow had been doing while she stood at the pocket, thirty-nine meters down, seal intact, her voice on the comms calm as a bank teller's.

The deck log had a hole in it too.

Not a dropout. She knew the shape the way she knew her own handwriting — flat walls, clean seam, two ends pressed together by a hand that knew precisely what it was doing. The same cut, lifted out. She dragged the playhead forward to find where the deck audio picked up again, and it didn't pick up at eleven seconds. It picked up fifty-two minutes later.

She sat with that. Fifty-two minutes of her own deck, gone. The wheelhouse mic had heard something last night, and a hand had reached into it and closed the two ends over the better part of an hour of the Marrow's life, and she had no memory of the hour on either side of the seam. She reached for it the way you reach for a word you know you know. Nothing. Not blur. Not the soft smear of a memory the deep had eaten. A clean edge. A wall.

She tried the pumps' own hour-counter. Cut. She tried the winch drum's revolutions, logged whether anyone asked or not. Cut. She tried her slate's battery draw, the crude trickle that ticked all night in the dark — it flatlined across the same window and resumed like a held breath let go. Every instrument on the boat that could have told her what she did last night had been gone into, one by one, and cut with the same patient hand.

And that was the thing that turned her cold, colder than the eleven seconds ever had. She rebuilt people for a living. She knew every redundant seam a slate kept, every stubborn stupid place a body writes itself down when it thinks no one's reading. To blind her own record this clean, you'd have had to know all of them. You'd have had to know her method well enough to beat it.

Nobody knew her method like she did.

She'd cut Sol tonight to spare the captain a truth — mercy, she'd told herself, the job, the kind lie. A minute ago she'd let the two holes match and taken comfort in it, the same cut twice, the same steady hand. *She'd cut the captain to be kind.* And it was a comfort, that symmetry, right up until it wasn't. Because a cut that spares someone else is a gift. A cut this thorough, aimed at the one person who could ever rebuild it, worked into her own suit and her own deck and her own pumps by a hand that knew exactly where she kept herself — that wasn't mercy done to her.

That was mercy she'd done to herself. To hide a thing she'd done. And the only thing on this coast worse than not knowing who you'd become was knowing, now, with the flat clean certainty of a seam pressed shut, that you'd looked at yourself last night and decided you'd be safer not remembering.
